questions.q: What was humanism, and how did it change European thought during the Renaissance?

answer.text: Humanism was a new way of thinking that developed during the Renaissance. It placed human beings, their reason, dignity and worldly life, at the centre of attention, in contrast to the earlier medieval emphasis on religion and the afterlife. Humanists revived the study of the classical texts of ancient Greece and Rome and stressed subjects like grammar, rhetoric, poetry, history and philosophy.

Humanism encouraged people to value individual talent and achievement, to observe the world for themselves, and to question old authorities. It promoted a spirit of curiosity, confidence in human ability, and an interest in living a full life in this world.
This outlook inspired new heights in art, literature and science, and laid the foundations of a more modern, secular way of thinking.

answer: Thus humanism marked a major shift in European culture.

questions.q: Discuss the achievements of the Renaissance in the fields of art and science.
answer: The Renaissance produced remarkable achievements in both art and science, often by the same gifted individuals.

answer.text: Renaissance artists achieved great realism by studying anatomy, geometry and the laws of perspective, so that their paintings and sculptures looked lifelike. Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa and the Last Supper, while Michelangelo created the statue of David and the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel, and Raphael too produced famous works.

In science, Copernicus put forward the bold idea that the Sun, not the Earth, was at the centre of the universe. This began a scientific revolution carried forward by Galileo, Kepler and Newton, who used observation and reason to understand nature.
The newly invented printing press helped these ideas spread quickly across Europe.

answer: Together, art and science gave the age its lasting brilliance.

questions.q: How did the invention of printing contribute to the changes of the Renaissance?

answer.text: developed in the fifteenth century, greatly accelerated the spread of Renaissance ideas.

list: Books could now be made quickly and cheaply, instead of being copied by hand
This spread the writings of humanists and the rediscovered works of ancient Greece and Rome to many readers
Literacy grew, and new ideas in science, religion and art circulated widely and quickly
Printing helped break the monopoly of the few over knowledge and prepared the ground for the Reformation and modern thought

questions.q: How did Renaissance ideas change people's view of the human being and the world?

answer.text: brought a new outlook that placed the human being and the present world at the centre of attention.

list: Humanism valued human reason, dignity and achievement, not only religious salvation
People took a fresh interest in this world — in nature, the body, and earthly life — rather than only the after-life
Artists studied anatomy and perspective to portray the human form realistically
Scholars observed nature directly, encouraging the scientific inquiry that would reshape the understanding of the universe
